nodes.title: Read me first
widgets_values:
# 4 - The score first

YuE2 writes a readable ABC score and then performs it. This splits the two.
**YuE2 Plan** writes the score and stops there; **YuE2 Render Plan** sings
whatever score it is handed.

## What it needs

The same YuE2-3B weights as template 2, 7.26 GB. Nothing extra.

## Why bother

The score is the last point at which a change is cheap, and it is the only
honest lever on where the stress of a line falls: capitalising a syllable
nudges the tokenizer, but editing the score moves the note.

Measured on an RTX 5090, two lines of lyrics, a 40-second ceiling: the whole
run took 8.9 s, of which the score was 2.2 s. Hunting for a seed one score
at a time costs a fraction of hunting one song at a time, and the saving
grows with length -- the singing gets longer, the score stays much the same.

## How to use it

1. Run. The score appears in the middle, the song on the right. With
   **score_abc** left empty the render sings the model's own score, and
   that is *byte for byte* the song template 2 makes from the same seed.
   Checked, not assumed.
2. For another tune, change the seed on **Write the score** and run again.
3. To change the tune yourself: copy the score out of the preview box,
   paste it into **score_abc** on the render node, edit it there and run.
   The score is not rewritten; only the singing runs again.

Changing one line -- `K:C` to `K:G` -- gives a different song, and a
different length with it. It does not give the same tune in G: every note
is read relative to the key, so each F is now sung as F-sharp and nothing
else moves. To move the whole song, connect an options node to the render
and set **transpose**, which moves every note and chord by the same step.

## What the options socket does here

An options node on the render overrides what the plan carried, with one
exception: `cot`. That decides what the model was told before it wrote the
score, so honouring a change here would sing one score under the
instructions written for another. The node says so rather than doing it.

## Where to go next

- **5 - Four scores, one song** -- four takes at once, chosen by ear.
- **6 - One take, both decoders** -- the same performance, decoded twice.
